source.title: Sparse Coding, for Mechanistic Interpretability and Activation Engineering

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse autoencoders to language models, reporting qualitative results for Pythia 70M and Llama-2 7B. It does not test the toy-network geometry or capacity mechanism directly.
record.gate_note: The post argues that superposition and capacity pressure explain polysemanticity, but does not experimentally test feature overlap, sparsity-dependent geometric transitions, importance, or capacity competition. Its own results are top-token visualizations of sparse-autoencoder directions, which the author describes as a naive interpretability measure. The cited MATS results and the comments are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The post trains L1-penalised sparse autoencoders on activations from real language models: Pythia 70M at layers 1–5 and Llama-2 7B at layer 13. It reports qualitative top-token evidence that the dictionary directions look like interpretable features. This bears on V4, that LLMs contain sparse features an SAE can recover, in a setting other than the toy-model original. The evidence is qualitative only: no ground truth, no reconstruction metrics, no controls.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author replicates the MATS Pythia 70M sparse-coding result and extends it to Llama-2 7B layer 13. He finds SAE directions interpretable by top tokens, unlike raw neurons. He calls the approach very promising and speculates it could in principle enumerate every concept a layer represents. He caveats possible code bugs, the naive top-token method and an under-explored sparsity range.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains L1-regularized sparse autoencoders on activations from real language models and interprets their directions through top-token visualizations; it does not reproduce the original toy-network experiments or their geometric measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability varies by layer: Pythia layers 1 and 2 are described as most interpretable, with later layers more garbled. Sparsity also matters: the Llama-2 7B layer-13 results use L0 approximately 60, and too-low sparsity is associated with token fixation. The author suggests there may not be a single best sparsity for all layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-token lists for ten raw Llama-2 7B layer-13 neurons look incoherent, used as a baseline against SAE directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Raw neurons in LLMs are less interpretable by top-token inspection than SAE dictionary directions.

record.problems: The evidence is qualitative and based on top-token visualizations, which the author calls naive. The author notes that the code may contain meaningful bugs, that the Llama-2 sparsity range was not thoroughly explored, and that later-layer interpretability is weaker. No ground-truth feature labels or controls are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The post includes long per-layer token lists beyond the ten directions shown for each Pythia layer and the longer Llama-2 layer-13 list in the footnotes. These additional directions were not extracted separately because they are the same qualitative measure and condition as the corresponding layer rows.

untested.parts: No toy networks; no geometry, near-orthogonality or sparsity-dependent phase transition.
Capacity pressure is invoked as theory only; feature importance and dedicated versus shared dimensions are not tested.
No investigation of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Does not measure how features are distributed across neurons. Does not validate SAE features causally or against labels. Reports no reconstruction loss.
The author speculates the SAE enumerates 'all of the features' but does not test completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicity.
Assumes 1-D directions; multidimensional features are not tested.

missing.what: Most Pythia SAE directions are dropped as all-negative or zero: only about 5 in 100 of 5120 directions are kept. This is a large dead or unused fraction, relevant to how many features the SAE actually recovers.
missing.locator: Footnote 4 (Pythia activations collected during six-shot TruthfulQA)

missing.what: For Llama-2 7B, L0≈20 is judged too low and L0≈60 is used. The author suggests no single best sparsity across layers.

record.verdict_notes: Blog post (LessWrong), not peer-reviewed. Data are small: TruthfulQA six-shot activations. All evidence is qualitative top-token lists with no metrics, reconstruction loss or controls. The comment by Charlie Steiner questions whether top tokens reflect features rather than token detectors. The cited MATS results are not this study's own.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test overlapping, nearly orthogonal feature geometry or a sparsity-dependent transition in toy networks.
Discusses capacity pressure as an explanation, but does not test whether importance or limited capacity causes dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Provides only qualitative top-token evidence; does not validate recovered features against labels, ground truth, or causal behavior.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable across settings, or canonical units of the model.
Uses individual SAE neuron directions, but does not test whether the model's underlying features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Trained a sparse autoencoder on layer activations and visualized top input tokens for its directions.

conditions.value: L0 target range given as 20 for smaller models; layer-specific value not stated

rows.measure: Top input tokens for listed SAE directions; qualitative interpretability
rows.value: Listed directions included token groups associated with concepts or patterns such as questions, people, numbers, and locations; the author says layers 1 and 2 are the most interpretable.
rows.locator: Autoencoder Interpretability — Pythia 70M; footnote Pythia 70M Autoencoder Data
rows.note: The text lists ten unsorted non-zero directions per layer and their top tokens. The measure is qualitative and does not independently establish feature identity.
rows.check: The author calls layers 1–2 the most interpretable. Listed directions are coherent (e.g. dim 124 'what/What', dim 1595 European cities). Qualitatively, the version's effect appears in full. Partial understates the author's own reading; the qualitative nature belongs in the verdict reason.

rows.subject: Llama-2 7B
rows.operation_detail: Trained a sparse autoencoder on layer activations and visualized top input tokens for its directions.
rows.measure: Top input tokens for listed SAE directions; qualitative interpretability
rows.value: The listed directions include token groups associated with topics or patterns such as artificial intelligence, England, statements, and program-related terms; the author says the dimensions appear semantically meaningful.
rows.locator: Autoencoder Interpretability — Llama-2 7B; footnote Llama-2 7B Autoencoder Data
rows.note: The post displays ten directions in the main section and a longer list in the footnote. The author says L0 approximately 20 seemed too low for this model and that the sparsity range needs more exploration.

rows.subject: Llama-2 7B
rows.operation_detail: Visualized top input tokens for model neurons without using the sparse autoencoder.
rows.measure: Top input tokens for ten model neurons
rows.value: The listed neurons' top-token groups are varied and do not provide an obvious, consistent interpretation in the post's examples.
rows.note: This is a top-token comparison, not a measurement of whether a feature is distributed across multiple neurons.
rows.check: Comparator only: top tokens of raw model neurons used as a baseline for r6. Kept unlinked because top-token lists don't measure distribution of features across neurons.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Observed top-token behavior in sparse autoencoders as sparsity was lowered.

conditions.value: too low; exact value not stated

rows.value: As sparsity is pushed too low, the autoencoders increasingly fixate on a particular token; for GPT-2 the token is described as esthetic.
rows.note: The post does not give the layer, sparsity value, or a quantified measure.
rows.check: No layer, sparsity value or quantity is given; it is an anecdotal footnote. It shows recovery degrading at too-low L0.

rows.subject: Llama-2 7B
rows.operation_detail: Observed top-token behavior in sparse autoencoders as sparsity was lowered.
rows.value: At this low sparsity, the autoencoder is reported to fixate on the beginning-of-sequence token.
rows.locator: Footnote on low-sparsity autoencoder behavior; linked token_info.csv
rows.note: The post gives the layer, approximate L0, and token, but does not quantify the fixation.

relationships.condition: Pythia 70M layers 1–2; Llama-2 7B layer 13 at L0≈60 (TruthfulQA activations, top-token interpretation)
relationships.reason: Author reports SAE directions with coherent top-token groups, unlike raw neurons. Evidence is qualitative only (r1, r2, r6).
relationships.display_finding: The author reports SAE directions with coherent top-token groups, unlike raw neurons; the evidence is qualitative.

relationships.condition: Pythia 70M layers 3–5; autoencoders with too-low L0 (GPT-2, Llama-2 7B layer 7 at L0≈20)
relationships.reason: Later layers are described as more garbled. Too-low sparsity makes SAEs fixate on single tokens ('esthetic', <s>), so recovery depends on layer and on the L0 choice (r3–r5, r8, r9).
relationships.display_finding: Later layers were described as more garbled. With too low an L0, the autoencoders fixated on single tokens such as 'esthetic' and <s>, so recovery depends on layer and L0 choice.
